hints: Start by orientating yourself on Fig. 6.1 - remember the heart is shown as if facing you, so the right side of the heart is on the left of the diagram. Trace where blood enters and leaves each chamber.

Think about function linked to structure - which valves sit at the exits of the ventricles into arteries, which artery receives blood directly from the thick-walled left ventricle, and which ventricle has to pump only a short distance to the lungs.
Look closely at S at the base of a large artery, P as the large arching vessel leaving the left side, and N as the thinner-walled lower chamber on the right side of the diagram.
walkthrough:
Spot the Semilunar Valve**
S points to pocket valves at the base of a great artery leaving a ventricle. These are semilunar valves. They snap shut when ventricular pressure falls, so blood in the artery cannot fall back into the ventricle. Atrioventricular valves like M are between atrium and ventricle, so S is the correct match.

Find the Highest Pressure Vessel**
The left ventricle has the thickest muscle wall labelled T because it must generate the highest pressure to push blood around the whole body. The vessel leaving it is the aorta. P is the aorta arching upwards, so P carries blood under highest pressure.

Find the Pump to the Lungs**
Blood returning from the body in L (vena cava) enters the right atrium, passes through M (tricuspid valve) into N. N is therefore the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood a short distance to the lungs via the pulmonary artery, so N is the chamber that pumps to the lungs.
Final answer: valve preventing back flow into a ventricle - S; blood vessel under highest pressure - P; chamber that pumps blood to lungs - N.

hints: Focus only on heart, vessels and blood - not on the brain effects of nicotine or long-term lung disease. What would make the heart work harder in the short term?
Think about two linked changes: the rate the heart beats and the pressure of blood in arteries. Then think about what nicotine does to vessel diameter and to the vessel lining.
For the third point, link vessel damage to blood clotting - what happens to platelets and the chance of a clot blocking a coronary artery?
walkthrough:
Heart Works Faster and Harder**
Nicotine quickly stimulates the cardiovascular system. Heart rate increases and blood pressure increases because the heart contracts more often and more forcefully and arterioles constrict. This raises the workload and oxygen demand of the heart muscle.

Vessels Constrict and Lining is Damaged**
Nicotine causes vasoconstriction, narrowing small arteries and arterioles, which further raises blood pressure. It also damages the endothelium, the smooth inner lining of vessels. A damaged lining is a starting point for atherosclerosis.

Blood More Likely to Clot**
Nicotine makes platelets stickier, so blood is more likely to clot and form a thrombus. Combined with narrowed vessels and endothelial damage, this greatly increases short-term risk of blockage of coronary arteries.
Final answer: Any three: increased heart rate; increased blood pressure; increased risk of blood clotting / thrombus formation; damages endothelium; vasoconstriction / reduced diameter of vessels.

hints: Recall the cell cycle order: nuclear division (mitosis) is followed by cytoplasm division (cytokinesis). What would a cell look like if it finished the first but never did the second?
walkthrough:
Mitosis Without Cytokinesis**
If the full cycle completes, one cell divides into two separate cells each with one nucleus. If the cycle stops at the end of mitosis, the nucleus has divided but the cytoplasm has not divided. The result is one larger adult myocyte containing two nuclei and twice the DNA / chromosome content.
Final answer: Cells stopped at end of mitosis have two nuclei / double DNA content because cytokinesis / cytoplasm division has not occurred, while completed cells have one nucleus.

hints: Think about what the cell cycle is for - making new cells. If most adult heart cells can no longer go through it, what process is now impossible when cells get old or damaged?
Link this to a heart attack or wear with age - if dead cardiac muscle cannot be replaced by new cardiac muscle, how must the heart repair the gap and why is that less good?
walkthrough:
No New Muscle Cells**
Stopping the cell cycle means adult cardiac myocytes cannot divide by mitosis to produce new myocytes. Old, worn out or damaged cells lost through normal ageing or after a heart attack cannot be replaced.

Poor Repair of the Heart**
Because new functional cardiac muscle cannot be made, damaged heart tissue cannot be properly regenerated. Any repair has to use non-contractile scar tissue, which does not contract and so weakens overall pumping ability of the heart.
Final answer: Unable to replace damaged / worn out / old cardiac myocytes; unable to repair damaged cardiac muscle / heart tissue, so repair is with unspecialised cells / scar tissue.
